title: Nonowantuck (Crystal Brook)
summary: Nonowantuck preserves a remembered Indigenous name for a creek in the Mount Sinai landscape. William Wallace Tooker associated it with Crystal Brook, a stream and valley on the harbor’s western side, while acknowledging that he had found no early written forms of the name.
why_this_matters: A creek can disappear or change while its name preserves knowledge of the landscape. Nonowantuck invites us to read Mount Sinai through Indigenous place naming as well as later English names, and to distinguish what a historical source records from what remains uncertain.
history_title: A Creek Name and a Changing Landscape
history_content:
Nonowantuck connects Indigenous language with a waterway that later writers knew as Crystal Brook. In 1911, William Wallace Tooker distinguished the original creek name from its later association with the wider Mount Sinai locality. He described a small stream running from the inland plains into the western side of the harbor and a valley that retained the Crystal Brook name.1

What the record can tell us

Tooker explicitly said he could not find early written forms of Nonowantuck and regarded the name as traditional. His account therefore preserves a remembered landscape; it does not establish a surveyed historic stream course. He also connected the colonial name “Old Man’s” with an Indigenous resident, citing seventeenth-century records. Those English labels do not tell us how that person identified himself.1
translation_content:
No separate spelling variants are listed in the available references. The name is interpreted as a creek that dries up or a dry creek, from a root connected with drying and the creek suffix -tuck.

Why Place Names Matter

“Some names carry the presence of ancestors, their journeys, their teachings, their conversations with the land. These names mark moments of connection, remembrance, and responsibility, kept alive through generations.”

— Native Land Digital, Indigenous Place Names (2024), The Story of Place is Alive section

A creek can disappear or change while its name preserves knowledge of the landscape. Nonowantuck invites us to read Mount Sinai through Indigenous place naming as well as later English names, and to distinguish what a historical source records from what remains uncertain.
whereintheworld_content: The marker gives broad orientation in the Crystal Brook area, on the western side of Mount Sinai Harbor, present-day Mount Sinai, NY. Tooker’s account supports this general landscape but cannot establish the former channel or a precise historic boundary. It is not a marked walking destination or permission to enter private property.1
